lines: A plain cell, holding a counter, touched by exactly one thread. Nothing about this is interesting yet, and that's the point.
The compiler already knows this type is safe to hand to another thread entirely. The open question is something different: is it safe to let two threads touch the same one, at once?
Wrap that same cell in a shared, reference counted pointer, clone the pointer, and hand the clone to a second thread.
Before either thread runs a single line, does this even build?
answer: No. The shared pointer's own atomic count only ever protects its own bookkeeping.
It adds no synchronization at all to the value sitting inside it, so sharing a cell through it is exactly as unsynchronized as sharing a bare cell would be.

lines: Notice which word is missing from both of these messages: neither one says the cell can't move to another thread at all.
Both say it can't be shared between two threads at once, and that's a sharper, different claim — the same single trait is doing all the work in both failures.
This is the one change that actually fixes what the cell couldn't: a real, synchronized gate around every single access.
Four threads hammer on it at once, and the total still comes out exact — not luck, just because only one thread is ever inside that gate at a time.
The counter itself crossed threads without trouble, locked. Now try handing the lock's own guard, the thing taking it hands back, to a second thread.

That one fails, and for a sharp reason: the guard is tied, by the platform's own locking rules, to the exact thread that took it. Handing it elsewhere would let another thread try to release a lock it never held.
A generic wrapper with an ordinary marker field simply inherits whatever its payload allows.
Swap that marker for a raw pointer instead, and the wrapper loses the ability to move to another thread no matter what it's holding — raw pointers never get that ability on their own.
A separate, hand built box can grant that ability right back, with one unsafe line the compiler trusts completely and can never check itself.
A spawned task creates a non atomic shared pointer, pauses once, and uses that same pointer again right after it resumes.
Does the whole task still qualify to be handed to the runtime at all?
answer: No. A spawned task has to qualify to cross threads in its entirety, not just the line that starts it.
It only qualifies when everything still alive at the exact moment it pauses also qualifies — and here, something that doesn't is still alive right there.

lines: Same pointer, same task. The only difference is whether it's still sitting there at the exact instant everything pauses.
Scope it away before that instant, and there is nothing left to check. Let it survive past that instant, and the whole task inherits its limitation.
Safe to move and safe to share turned out to be two separate questions, both answered the same structural way: look at a type's own fields.
A lock's guard stays loyal to the thread that took it. And only two deliberate overrides exist anywhere in this picture, pointed in opposite directions.
